tip: 'Que ce soit clair' = 'let it be clear.' A sentence-starting Que + subjunctive (soit) fires off a wish or order, where English reaches for 'let' or 'may.'
'Concours' normally means a competition or contest – but in formal French it means help or support. 'Votre concours' here is your assistance, not a contest.
'Ménager la chèvre et le chou' is literally 'spare the goat and the cabbage' – feed the goat without letting it eat the cabbage. Means please both sides.
After a superlative, French switches to the subjunctive: 'le plus beau... que j'aie jamais vu' takes aie, not ai. Same after seul, premier, dernier.
Literally 'circling around the pot,' where English beats around the bush – both mean stalling instead of getting to the point.
'Mettre son grain de sel' is literally 'to add your grain of salt' – but it means butting in with an unasked opinion, not the English skepticism sense.
'Tout brillant qu'il soit' = 'however brilliant he may be.' Tout + adjective + que takes the subjunctive (soit) to concede a point.
'Ça passe crème' is youth slang – literally 'it passes like cream,' meaning it'll go off smoothly, no hitch.
'Faire la grasse matinée' is literally 'to do the fat morning' – French for a lazy lie-in, sleeping well past your alarm.
'Casser trois pattes à un canard' is literally 'break three legs off a duck' – hardly a feat, since a duck has two. Means nothing special, no big deal.
'Avoir d'autres chats à fouetter' is literally 'other cats to whip,' where English has 'other fish to fry' – both mean more pressing things to deal with.
'Raconter des salades' is literally 'to tell salads' – a jumble of tossed leaves standing in for a jumble of made-up stories. Informal.
French clears 'un chat dans la gorge' – a cat in the throat – where English has a frog. Same tickly, hoarse feeling.
'Bonnet blanc et blanc bonnet' is just 'white hat' and 'hat white' – the same two words flipped, so the two options are literally identical.
'Se faire un ciné' = 'let's catch a movie.' Se faire un + noun is the casual 'go grab a...' frame: se faire un resto, un café.
'Je me permets de' is literally 'I permit myself to' – the stock polite hedge that opens a formal French letter before you make a request.
'Par la présente' means 'hereby' – literally 'by the present,' i.e. by this very letter. The standard opener of a formal notice.
'Mettre les bouchées doubles' is literally 'to take double mouthfuls' – eating twice as fast becomes working twice as hard.
'Vendre la mèche' is literally 'to sell the fuse' – handing over the fuse betrays the plot before the charge can blow. Means to spill a secret.
'Tomber dans le panneau' – panneau was once a hunter's net, so you literally fall into the trap. Means to fall for the trick.
'Une autre paire de manches' is literally 'another pair of sleeves' – sleeves were once detachable, a separate garment to sort out. Means a whole different matter.
'Tirer son épingle du jeu' is literally 'to pull your pin out of the game' – walking away with your stake intact. Means to come out of it well.
'Mettre les pieds dans le plat' is literally 'to put both feet in the dish' – French goes bigger than English 'put your foot in it.' Means to blunder in tactlessly.
For a plural 'it's THEM who...,' French uses ce sont, not c'est: 'ce sont eux qui ont pris.' The verb agrees with the plural.
'Si grand que soit le défi' = 'however great the challenge.' Si + adjective + que takes the subjunctive (soit) to mean 'however X.'
'Tomba' is the literary past of tomber, used in narration in place of 'est tombé.' The passé simple carries no helper verb at all.
'À peine fut-il sorti que' = 'barely had he left when.' Fronting à peine flips subject and verb (fut-il), just like the English inversion.
'Rares sont les occasions' fronts the adjective for emphasis, flipping verb and subject – literally 'rare are the chances.'
'Eut pleuré' is the literary past-in-the-past, standing in for 'avait pleuré' after après que. You'll meet it only in written narration.
'Cherchez la femme' – 'look for the woman' – comes from Dumas: the notion that a woman is behind whatever tangle you're puzzling over.
Literally 'those who resemble each other gather together' – and ressemble/assemble rhyme, which is why the proverb lodges in your head.
'Demeure entière' is literally 'remains whole' – not one part of the question has been answered. Formal register.
'Habit' here is a false friend: French habit means a garment – the monk's robe – not a routine. Literally 'the robe doesn't make the monk.'
'Nous nous garderons de' is literally 'we'll guard ourselves from' – the reflexive turns 'guard' into 'refrain from.' Formal caution.
'Force m'est de' means 'I'm compelled to' – literally 'force is upon me to,' where the m' marks who has no choice. Very formal.
That 'serait' (would be), not 'est' (is), softens the claim – French academic writing hedges with the conditional to sound less absolute.
'Nous nous attacherons à' is literally 'we'll attach ourselves to' demonstrating – the reflexive image means to commit to the task. Formal.
'Pallier' takes a direct object: 'pallier les insuffisances,' never 'pallier à' – unlike remédier à. Even native speakers slip on this one.
'Ont toujours tort' – avoir tort is literally 'to have wrong.' French uses 'have,' not 'be,' for being at fault, and the absent always cop the blame.
'Petit à petit' = 'little by little.' French doubles a word around à for a step-by-step feel: peu à peu, côte à côte, goutte à goutte.
'Loin des yeux, loin du cœur' is literally 'far from the eyes, far from the heart' – where English says 'out of sight, out of mind'.
'À bon chat, bon rat' is literally 'to a good cat, a good rat' – a sharp attacker meets an equally sharp defender. Evenly matched.
'Errare humanum est' is Latin – 'to err is human' – dropped whole into formal French. It often continues: perseverare diabolicum (to persist, diabolical).
